usage: What you file at a police station or station office when you lose something.
Verb form; more formal/written than 잃어버리다 in spoken use.
물 here means 'object'; 분실물 센터 = lost & found center.
Very common combo — put the noun before 분실.
examples: 지하철에서 지갑을 분실했어요.
I lost my wallet on the subway.
분실하다 sounds appropriately formal when reporting.
분실 신고를 하려고 하는데요.
I'd like to file a lost-item report.
-(으)려고 하는데요 softly opens a request at a counter.
분실물 센터가 몇 층에 있어요?
What floor is the lost & found on?
Useful at big stations and department stores.
nuance: 분실 is the noun the system uses on signs and forms; in casual speech people still say 잃어버렸어요. Use 분실 when talking to officials, writing a report, or reading signage like 분실물 보관소. It implies you misplaced your own item, not that someone took it.
mistakes: Don't confuse 분실 (you lost it) with 도난 (it was stolen) — police treat them very differently.
분실 is a noun; to make it a verb add 하다 (분실하다), don't just say 분실해요 about a person.

usage: Filed when an item is taken by someone, unlike 분실.
당하다 marks you as the victim of the action.
Often seen in notices warning residents.
방지 = prevention; common on locks and tags.
examples: 자전거를 도난당했어요.
My bike got stolen.
도난당하다 is the natural verb when you're the victim.
도난 신고를 하러 경찰에 왔어요.
I came to the police to report a theft.
Pair 도난 with 신고 at the station.
요즘 이 동네에 택배 도난이 많대요.
They say there's a lot of parcel theft in this neighborhood lately.
-대요 reports something you heard.
nuance: 도난 specifically means someone took your property, so police open a criminal case rather than just logging a lost item. Use 도난당하다 to say you were the victim; saying plain 도난했어요 wrongly sounds like you did the stealing. It is more formal than the everyday 훔쳐 갔어요.
mistakes: Never say 도난했어요 to mean 'I was robbed' — that reads as 'I committed theft'; use 도난당했어요.
도난 (stolen) is not 분실 (misplaced); using the wrong one changes whether police investigate.

usage: The single most common compound — write it as one word.
나다 is the natural intransitive verb for accidents.
내다 marks you as the one at fault.
현장 = the spot where it happened.
examples: 방금 앞에서 교통사고가 났어요.
There was just a traffic accident up ahead.
사고가 나다 = an accident occurs, no one blamed yet.
제가 사고를 내서 보험사에 전화했어요.
I caused an accident, so I called the insurance company.
사고를 내다 admits fault.
사고가 나면 먼저 112에 신고하세요.
If there's an accident, report it to 112 first.
112 is the police line; 119 is fire/ambulance.
nuance: 사고 covers car crashes, workplace mishaps, and any sudden harmful event. The key contrast is 사고가 나다 (it happened) versus 사고를 내다 (you caused it) — Koreans listen closely to which you use. For a fender-bender people often add 접촉사고 (minor collision).
mistakes: Don't mix up 사고가 났어요 (an accident happened) with 사고를 냈어요 (I caused one) — the second admits liability.
사고 is the event; the injured person is a 피해자, not a 사고.

usage: Used for accidents, disputes, and out-of-court deals.
The amount paid to settle, esp. after an accident.
서 = written document you both sign.
보다 here means 'to work out' an agreement.
examples: 상대방하고 합의를 봤어요.
I reached a settlement with the other party.
합의를 보다 is the everyday phrasing.
합의금으로 백만 원을 받았어요.
I received one million won as a settlement.
합의금 is the payout amount.
경찰서에서 합의서를 작성했어요.
We filled out the settlement agreement at the police station.
Often signed before charges are dropped.
nuance: 합의 is huge in Korean accident and minor-crime culture: reaching 합의 with the victim often reduces or drops a case. It implies both sides agreed, usually with money (합의금) changing hands. Don't confuse it with a casual 'agreement' on plans — that's more like 약속 or 동의.
mistakes: 합의 (legal/financial settlement) is not 동의 (agreeing with an opinion) — keep them separate.
Saying 합의했어요 implies a deal is final; if you're still negotiating, say 합의 중이에요.

usage: 내다 is the verb for paying penalties and fees.
형 = a type of criminal sentence.
State the amount right after 벌금.
고지서 = the official payment slip you receive.
examples: 음주운전으로 벌금을 냈어요.
I paid a fine for drunk driving.
벌금 attaches to actual offenses.
벌금이 생각보다 많이 나왔어요.
The fine came out higher than I expected.
나오다 = (a charge) is issued.
벌금 고지서가 집으로 왔어요.
The fine notice came to my house.
고지서 arrives by mail.
nuance: 벌금 is a criminal-court fine for an actual offense, so it goes on a different track than 과태료 (an administrative penalty for minor rule-breaking). Koreans distinguish them sharply: a 벌금 means you were found to have committed a crime. Always pair it with 내다 (to pay), not 주다.
mistakes: Don't swap 벌금 (criminal fine) with 과태료 (admin penalty like illegal parking) — they have different legal weight.
Use 벌금을 내다, not 벌금을 주다; 주다 sounds like you're giving money away as a gift.

usage: The most common reason residents get one.
부과 = the act of charging it to you.
The slip mailed to you with the amount.
examples: 불법 주차로 과태료가 나왔어요.
I got a fine for illegal parking.
Very typical for car owners in the city.
과태료는 인터넷으로도 낼 수 있어요.
You can also pay the fine online.
Many fines are payable on government sites.
기한 안에 내면 과태료가 깎여요.
If you pay within the deadline, the fine is reduced.
Early payment often gets a discount.
nuance: 과태료 is a lighter, administrative penalty for breaking minor rules — illegal parking, late registration, missed reporting — and it does not make you a criminal. Compare 벌금, which is a court fine for an actual offense. Residents meet 과태료 most often through parking and the late 전입신고.
mistakes: 과태료 (admin penalty) is not 벌금 (criminal fine); confusing them overstates how serious the violation is.
It's 과태료, not 과대료 — the middle syllable is 태, easy to misspell.

english: civil complaint / public petition or request
usage: 넣다 = to put in (submit) a 민원.
What the office does when it receives your 민원.
실 = the room/desk that handles public requests.
The current online portal (it absorbed the old 민원24) where many 민원 are filed.
examples: 주민센터에 민원을 넣었어요.
I filed a request at the community center.
민원을 넣다 is the everyday verb.
층간소음 때문에 민원이 많이 들어와요.
A lot of complaints come in about noise between floors.
들어오다 = (complaints) come in.
민원실은 1층 오른쪽에 있어요.
The civil affairs window is on the right on the first floor.
Handy when navigating a 구청.
nuance: 민원 covers any official request or complaint a citizen makes to a public office — issuing documents, reporting a problem, asking the 구청 to fix something. It's a core word for dealing with Korean bureaucracy. Note it can be a neutral request, not only a complaint, so context decides the tone.
mistakes: 민원 (request to a public office) is broader than a mere 불만 (dissatisfaction) — it's the formal channel, not just grumbling.
Use 민원을 넣다 or 제기하다, not 민원을 하다, which sounds incomplete.

usage: Proves you work somewhere; needed for visas, loans.
떼다 is the idiomatic verb for pulling official docs.
발급 = official issuing; seen on kiosks and sites.
Proof of earnings, often for rent or visas.
examples: 재직증명서를 한 통 떼야 해요.
I need to get one copy of an employment certificate.
통 is the counter for documents/letters.
증명서는 무인 발급기에서 뽑을 수 있어요.
You can print certificates at the self-service kiosk.
무인 발급기 = unmanned issuing machine.
은행에서 소득증명서를 요구했어요.
The bank asked for an income certificate.
Common when opening accounts or loans.
nuance: 증명서 is the catch-all suffix for official proof documents (재직-, 소득-, 출입국사실-증명서). The verb 떼다 — literally 'to detach' — is how Koreans say 'get a copy' of one, which surprises learners. Many can now be issued at kiosks or on 정부24 without visiting a counter.
mistakes: 증명서 (a proof document) is not the same as 신분증 (an ID card) — don't use them interchangeably.
Say 증명서를 떼다 or 발급받다; learners often wrongly say 증명서를 만들다 (to make one yourself).

usage: Seen on accident-area posters seeking witnesses.
진술 = the account a witness gives police.
The verb form of seeing an event happen.
examples: 혹시 사고 목격자세요?
Are you by any chance a witness to the accident?
혹시 softens a direct question to a stranger.
목격자가 있어서 처리가 빨랐어요.
There was a witness, so it was handled quickly.
Witnesses speed up claims and reports.
제가 그 사고를 목격했어요.
I witnessed that accident.
목격하다 = to have seen it happen.
nuance: 목격자 is the person who actually saw an incident, a key word around accidents and crime reports. You'll see 목격자를 찾습니다 (seeking witnesses) signs near 교통사고 spots. The verb 목격하다 is more formal than 봤어요 and signals you saw something report-worthy.
mistakes: 목격자 (eyewitness) is not 피해자 (victim) — a witness saw it but wasn't harmed.
목격하다 is for incidents/events; don't use it for casually 'seeing' a friend — that's just 보다.

usage: The harmed party in an accident or crime.
The opposite role; learn the pair together.
입다 = to sustain (damage); root noun is 피해.
examples: 저는 이 사고의 피해자예요.
I'm the victim of this accident.
Establishes your role when reporting.
가해자가 보험으로 처리해 준대요.
The at-fault party says they'll handle it through insurance.
Contrast 가해자 with 피해자.
피해를 입은 만큼 보상을 받을 수 있어요.
You can get compensation in proportion to the harm suffered.
-(으)ㄴ 만큼 = to the extent that.
nuance: 피해자 (the harmed party) pairs with 가해자 (the one who caused harm); knowing which you are shapes everything in an accident or dispute. The base noun 피해 means damage/harm and combines widely: 피해를 입다, 피해 보상. It's standard, neutral legal vocabulary, not dramatic.
mistakes: Don't mix 피해자 (victim) with 가해자 (at-fault party) — reversing them flips who owes whom.
Use 피해를 입다 for suffering damage; 피해를 받다 is less natural in this fixed pairing.

usage: What you do when explaining events to police.
서 = the document recording your account.
A witness's account of the incident.
examples: 경찰서에서 진술서를 작성했어요.
I wrote out a statement at the police station.
진술서 + 작성하다 is the set phrase.
사실대로 진술하시면 됩니다.
You just need to state it truthfully.
사실대로 = as it really is; -(으)시면 됩니다 reassures.
통역사를 통해 진술했어요.
I gave my statement through an interpreter.
A right worth knowing as a foreigner — you can request one.
nuance: 진술 is your formal account of what happened, given to police or in writing as a 진술서. It's more weighty than just 말하다 because it can become evidence. As a foreign resident, remember you can ask for a 통역사 (interpreter) before you 진술하다.
mistakes: 진술 (formal statement to authorities) is heavier than 설명 (a casual explanation) — use it only in official contexts.
It's 진술, not 진실 (truth) — similar sound, different word; 진술서 ≠ 진실서.

usage: 받다 marks you as the one penalized.
examples: 음주운전은 강하게 처벌받아요.
Drunk driving is punished severely.
처벌받다 from the offender's side.
처벌을 원하지 않는다고 진술했어요.
I stated that I don't want them punished.
A real choice that can drop minor cases.
불법 주정차도 처벌 대상이에요.
Illegal parking is also subject to penalty.
대상이다 = to be a target/subject of.
nuance: 처벌 is the legal penalty itself — fines, sentences — and pairs with crimes and serious violations. A culturally important phrase is 처벌을 원하지 않는다 (I don't wish them punished), which a 피해자 can state to soften a case. Use 처벌받다 when you're the one penalized, 처벌하다 for the authority acting.
mistakes: Don't say 처벌했어요 about yourself when you mean you were punished — that's 처벌받았어요.
처벌 (legal punishment) is not 벌금 (a fine); a 벌금 is one form of 처벌, not the whole concept.
